data.title: Atopic dermatitis — viva
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Atopic dermatitis** (Eczemas)_

**Q1. Define atopy and atopic dermatitis.**
- Atopy: genetic tendency to produce IgE against common environmental allergens, with asthma, allergic rhinitis, conjunctivitis, AD, food allergy
- Atopic dermatitis: chronic relapsing intensely itchy inflammatory skin disease with typical age-related distribution, often first sign of the 'atopic march'

**Q2. Epidemiology?**
- 15–20% of children and 2–5% of adults worldwide (lower but rising in India); 60% begin in first year, 85% by 5 years
- Many improve by adolescence; adult-onset or persistent forms recognised

**Q3. Explain the pathogenesis (outside-in and inside-out).**
- Barrier defect: filaggrin (FLG) loss-of-function mutations (strongest genetic risk), reduced ceramides, increased TEWL, alkaline pH, kallikrein (KLK5/7) overactivity (SPINK5) → allergen and microbe entry
- Immune dysregulation: acute Th2 (IL-4, IL-13, IL-31), Th22 (IL-22) and in chronic phase Th1/Th17; keratinocyte alarmins TSLP, IL-33, IL-25; IgE sensitisation
- Microbiome: reduced diversity, S. aureus colonisation (superantigens, δ-toxin); Malassezia (head-neck)
- Itch: IL-31, IL-4/13 act on sensory neurons, histamine-independent — itch-scratch cycle

**Q4. Write a short note on filaggrin (PYQ).**
- 'Filament aggregating protein' — derived from profilaggrin in keratohyaline granules; aggregates keratin filaments in the stratum corneum and is broken down into natural moisturising factor (urocanic acid, pyrrolidone carboxylic acid) that hydrates and acidifies skin
- FLG mutations (R501X, 2282del4) cause ichthyosis vulgaris and increase risk of AD, asthma (with AD), peanut allergy and contact sensitisation; Indian mutations differ

**Q5. What are the Hanifin and Rajka criteria?**
- Major (need ≥3 of 4): pruritus; typical morphology and distribution (flexural lichenification in adults, facial and extensor in infants); chronic or chronically relapsing dermatitis; personal or family history of atopy
- Minor (need ≥3 of 23): xerosis, ichthyosis/palmar hyperlinearity/keratosis pilaris, immediate skin-test reactivity, raised IgE, early age of onset, tendency to skin infections, non-specific hand/foot dermatitis, nipple eczema, cheilitis, recurrent conjunctivitis, Dennie–Morgan fold, keratoconus, anterior subcapsular cataract, orbital darkening, facial pallor/erythema, pityriasis alba, anterior neck folds, itch when sweating, wool/lipid-solvent intolerance, perifollicular accentuation, food intolerance, course influenced by environment/emotions, white dermographism/delayed blanch

**Q6. What are the UK Working Party criteria?**
- Must have itchy skin (or parental report of scratching) in last 12 months, plus ≥3 of: history of flexural involvement (cheeks in <10 y), personal history of asthma/hay fever (or first-degree relative in <4 y), generally dry skin in last year, visible flexural eczema (cheeks/forehead/outer limbs in <4 y), onset before 2 years (not used if <4 y)
- Simpler, validated for epidemiology

**Q7. Describe the phases of AD.**
- Infantile (2 months–2 years): face (cheeks, sparing nose — 'headlight sign'), scalp, extensors; oozing, crusting; napkin area often spared
- Childhood (2–12 years): flexures (antecubital, popliteal), wrists, ankles, neck; lichenification, excoriation
- Adolescent/adult: flexures, face and neck ('head-and-neck dermatitis'), hands, eyelids, nipples; prurigo-like and lichenified
- Variants: nummular, follicular (common in darker skin), prurigo form, erythrodermic, juvenile plantar dermatosis, pityriasis alba

**Q8. What are the stigmata of atopy?**
- Dennie–Morgan infraorbital fold, Hertoghe's sign (thinning of lateral eyebrows), periorbital darkening, palmar hyperlinearity, keratosis pilaris, white dermographism, pityriasis alba, anterior neck folds, Hertoghe's, keratoconus and cataract

**Q9. Complications of AD.**
- Bacterial: impetiginisation (S. aureus), cellulitis
- Viral: eczema herpeticum (emergency), eczema molluscatum, eczema vaccinatum, eczema coxsackium
- Fungal: Malassezia head-neck dermatitis
- Erythroderma, growth retardation, sleep loss, psychosocial impact, ocular (keratoconus, cataract, conjunctivitis — also with dupilumab), contact allergy to topical agents, steroid side effects

**Q10. How do you assess severity?**
- SCORAD (extent by rule of nines, intensity of 6 signs 0–3, subjective itch and sleep 0–10 each; >50 severe), EASI (0–72; area × intensity in 4 regions), IGA, POEM (patient-oriented), DLQI/CDLQI for quality of life

**Q11. Investigations — are they needed?**
- Diagnosis is clinical
- Total IgE and eosinophils (raised in extrinsic AD), specific IgE/skin prick tests only if history suggests food allergy (avoid indiscriminate elimination diets)
- Swab for culture in infected eczema; Tzanck/PCR for suspected eczema herpeticum
- Patch test for suspected contact allergy (topical medicaments, emollients)
- Biopsy if diagnosis doubtful (CTCL in adult-onset)

**Q12. Differential diagnosis in infants and adults.**
- Infants: seborrhoeic dermatitis (greasy, folds, non-itchy, early), scabies, Netherton syndrome, Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome, hyper-IgE syndrome, SCID/Omenn, zinc deficiency, LCH, phenylketonuria
- Adults: contact dermatitis, psoriasis, CTCL (mycosis fungoides, Sézary), drug eruption, dermatitis herpetiformis, scabies, seborrhoeic dermatitis, photodermatoses

**Q13. Write a short note on Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome (PYQ).**
- X-linked recessive WAS gene mutation: triad of eczema, thrombocytopenia with small platelets (bleeding, petechiae) and recurrent infections (pyogenic, opportunistic); risk of lymphoma and autoimmunity; cure by haematopoietic stem cell transplant / gene therapy

**Q14. Management principles — stepwise.**
- Education, written action plan, avoid triggers (soaps, wool, sweat, heat, stress, dust mites), nails short
- Emollients liberally (≥250–500 g/week in adults), bath oils, soap substitutes; ceramide-dominant moisturisers
- Topical corticosteroids: right potency for site/age, fingertip-unit dosing, once daily; proactive twice-weekly application to healed areas to prevent flares
- Topical calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus 0.03%/0.1%, pimecrolimus 1%) — face, eyelids, flexures, steroid-sparing; burning at start
- Topical PDE4 inhibitor (crisaborole), topical JAK inhibitors (ruxolitinib cream), tapinarof
- Wet wraps for severe flares; dilute bleach baths for recurrent infections
- Phototherapy: narrow-band UVB, UVA1
- Systemic: cyclosporine 3–5 mg/kg/day (fast, short-term), methotrexate 7.5–25 mg weekly, azathioprine (check TPMT), mycophenolate; systemic steroids only short bridging
- Biologics: dupilumab (anti-IL-4Rα), tralokinumab and lebrikizumab (anti-IL-13), nemolizumab (anti-IL-31RA)
- Oral JAK inhibitors: baricitinib, upadacitinib, abrocitinib (monitor lipids, blood counts, infections, thrombosis)
- Antihistamines: sedating ones at night only for sleep; non-sedating have little effect on AD itch

**Q15. What is the role of diet and allergy testing?**
- Food allergy relevant mainly in infants with moderate–severe AD (egg, milk, peanut, wheat, soy); confirm by history + specific IgE/prick test ± oral food challenge
- Unnecessary elimination diets cause malnutrition; early introduction of peanut/egg reduces allergy (LEAP study)

**Q16. What is the atopic march?**
- Sequence: AD in infancy → food allergy → asthma → allergic rhinitis; barrier dysfunction allows epicutaneous sensitisation
- Early emollient use for prevention showed inconsistent results

**Q17. What is eczema herpeticum and how do you treat it?**
- Disseminated HSV on eczematous skin — monomorphic punched-out erosions, crusts, fever; urgent oral/IV acyclovir, stop topical steroid briefly/treat secondary infection, eye check

**Q18. Fingertip unit (FTU) concept.**
- Amount of cream from a 5 mm tube squeezed from the tip to the first crease of the index finger ≈ 0.5 g — covers two adult palms (2% BSA)
- Adult: face/neck 2.5 FTU, one arm 3, hand 1, one leg 6, foot 2, front trunk 7, back 7

**Q19. Side effects of topical steroids.**
- Atrophy, striae, telangiectasia, purpura, steroid rosacea/perioral dermatitis, acneiform eruption, hypertrichosis, tinea incognito, contact allergy, tachyphylaxis, glaucoma/cataract (eyelids), HPA suppression and growth retardation (children, potent and extensive use)
- Topical steroid addiction/withdrawal (red skin syndrome) on face/genitals with prolonged misuse

**Q20. How does dupilumab work and what are its side effects?**
- Monoclonal antibody against IL-4 receptor α — blocks both IL-4 and IL-13 signalling
- Adults and children ≥6 months; 600 mg loading then 300 mg every 2 weeks SC (adults)
- Side effects: conjunctivitis/keratitis, injection-site reactions, facial erythema (head-neck dermatitis), eosinophilia, arthralgia; no lab monitoring needed

**Q21. Prognosis?**
- Most childhood AD improves; poor prognostic factors: early onset severe disease, FLG mutations, associated asthma/rhinitis, family history, female sex, adult persistence, hand eczema in adulthood (wet work)

## Quick spotter facts
- Infant cheeks + scalp, nose spared — infantile AD
- Dennie–Morgan fold, Hertoghe's sign — atopic stigmata
- FLG mutation — ichthyosis vulgaris and AD

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Atopic dermatitis); Hanifin & Rajka and UK Working Party criteria; Indian consensus on AD. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
